content: More than two-thirds of pregnant women experience low-back pain, and nearly one-fifth report pelvic pain. These conditions may occur independently or together, and their prevalence typically increases as pregnancy progresses. This often interferes with work, daily activities, and sleep. The objective of this review was to update the evidence on the effects of various interventions aimed at preventing and treating low-back pain, pelvic pain, or both during pregnancy. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they evaluated any treatment or combination of treatments designed to prevent or reduce the incidence or severity of these conditions, as well as related functional disability, sick leave, and adverse effects. The review included 34 RCTs involving 5,121 pregnant women aged 16 to 45 years, with gestational ages ranging from 12 to 38 weeks when reported. Of these, 15 trials focused on low-back pain (1,847 participants), six on pelvic pain (889 participants), and 13 on both low-back and pelvic pain (2,385 participants). Two studies investigated the prevention of low-back pain, and four examined the prevention of both low-back and pelvic pain. Diagnoses ranged from self-reported symptoms to clinical interpretations based on specific tests. All interventions were provided in addition to usual prenatal care and were compared to usual prenatal care unless otherwise specified. For low-back pain, meta-analyses provided low-quality evidence that land-based exercise significantly reduced pain (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.03 to -0.25; 645 participants; seven studies) and functional disability (SMD -0.56; 95% CI -0.89 to -0.23; 146 participants; two studies). However, low-quality evidence also suggested no significant difference in the number of women reporting low-back pain when group exercise, combined with pain management information, was compared to usual prenatal care (risk ratio [RR] 0.97; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.17; 374 participants; two studies). For pelvic pain, meta-analyses provided low-quality evidence that there was no significant difference in the number of women reporting pelvic pain when group exercise, combined with pain management information, was compared to usual prenatal care (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.23; 374 participants; two studies). For combined low-back and pelvic pain, moderate-quality evidence suggested that an 8to 12-week exercise program reduced the number of women reporting these conditions (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.97; 1,176 participants; four studies). Land-based exercise in various formats also significantly reduced sick leave related to low-back and pelvic pain (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; 1,062 participants; two studies). However, due to clinical heterogeneity, results from individual studies evaluating other interventions could not be pooled. Moderate-quality evidence from individual studies suggested that osteomanipulative therapy significantly reduced low-back pain and functional disability, while acupuncture or craniosacral therapy improved pelvic pain more effectively than usual prenatal care. Evidence from individual studies, which was largely of low quality, also suggested that a multi-modal intervention (manual therapy, exercise, and education) significantly reduced pain and functional disability, though it did not significantly reduce sick leave. Reported adverse effects were minor and transient. In conclusion, there is low-quality evidence that exercise, whether on land or in water, may reduce pregnancy-related low-back pain. Moderateto low-quality evidence suggests that exercise improves functional disability and reduces sick leave more effectively than usual prenatal care. Evidence from individual studies indicates that acupuncture or craniosacral therapy may improve pregnancy-related pelvic pain, and osteomanipulative therapy or multi-modal interventions may also be beneficial. However, clinical heterogeneity limited the ability to pool results in many cases, and substantial statistical heterogeneity was observed in all but three meta-analyses. Publication bias and selective reporting cannot be ruled out. Further research is needed to improve confidence in these findings and refine treatment approaches. The development of a standardized classification system to categorize women based on their symptoms could help tailor treatments more effectively.
